concepts.definition: Working out what can go wrong before you build it, not after.
concepts.name: Threat Modeling

concepts.definition: One-way fingerprints: the same input always gives the same digest, and there is no way back.
concepts.name: Cryptographic Hashing

concepts.definition: One shared key both locks and unlocks — fast, and only as safe as the key.
concepts.name: Symmetric Encryption

concepts.definition: Two keys, one of them public: how strangers agree on a secret in the open.
concepts.name: Public-Key Cryptography

concepts.definition: How a browser gets a private, authenticated channel to a server it has never met.
concepts.name: TLS & Certificates

concepts.definition: Establishing who is making the request — passwords, passkeys, MFA.
concepts.name: Authentication

concepts.definition: Salted, deliberately slow hashes: the difference between a breach and a catastrophe.
concepts.name: Password Storage

concepts.definition: What an authenticated identity is allowed to do once it is through the door.
concepts.name: Authorization

concepts.definition: Every account and process gets the smallest set of rights that still works.
concepts.name: Least Privilege

concepts.definition: The field's shared list of the ways web applications actually get broken.
concepts.name: OWASP Top Ten

concepts.definition: Cookies, tokens and expiry — where a login is kept after the password is gone.
concepts.name: Session Management

concepts.definition: Untrusted input reaching the database as code rather than as data.
concepts.name: SQL Injection

concepts.definition: Attacker script running in your user's browser with your site's privileges.
concepts.name: Cross-Site Scripting

concepts.definition: Another site making your user's already-authenticated browser act on your behalf.
concepts.name: Cross-Site Request Forgery

concepts.definition: Persuading the server to fetch a URL the attacker chose, from inside your network.
concepts.name: Server-Side Request Forgery

concepts.definition: The browser rule that keeps sites apart, and the header that relaxes it on purpose.
concepts.name: Same-Origin Policy & CORS

concepts.definition: Telling the browser exactly what it is allowed to load and run.
concepts.name: Content Security Policy

concepts.definition: Decide what is acceptable on the way in; escape it for its destination on the way out.
concepts.name: Input Validation & Output Encoding

concepts.definition: Mapping a target's attack surface before touching any of it.
concepts.name: Reconnaissance

concepts.definition: Attacking the human layer — phishing is still how most intrusions start.
concepts.name: Social Engineering

concepts.definition: Automated sweeps for known weaknesses: breadth, not depth.
concepts.name: Vulnerability Scanning

concepts.definition: A scoped, authorized attempt to actually get in, and a report of how.
concepts.name: Penetration Testing

concepts.definition: Buffer overflows and use-after-free: what happens when code trusts a length.
concepts.name: Memory Corruption

concepts.definition: Throwing malformed input at software until it misbehaves, then keeping the input that did.
concepts.name: Fuzzing

concepts.definition: Turning a crash into controlled execution.
concepts.name: Exploit Development

concepts.definition: Turning the foothold you have into the access you wanted.
concepts.name: Privilege Escalation

concepts.definition: An adversarial exercise against the whole organization, defenders included.
concepts.name: Red-Teaming

concepts.definition: You can only detect what something bothered to record.
concepts.name: Logging & Telemetry

concepts.definition: Seeing what a running system is doing from the outside, without shipping a new build.
concepts.name: Observability

concepts.definition: A shared vocabulary for what attackers actually do, technique by technique.
concepts.name: MITRE ATT&CK

concepts.definition: One place every log lands, where rules and queries run across all of it.
concepts.name: SIEM

concepts.definition: Knowing which adversaries are aimed at you, and how they operate.
concepts.name: Threat Intelligence

concepts.definition: Writing and tuning the rules that turn telemetry into alerts worth waking someone for.
concepts.name: Detection Engineering

concepts.definition: The rehearsed sequence from alert to containment to recovery.
concepts.name: Incident Response

concepts.definition: Reconstructing what happened from disk, memory and logs the attacker left behind.
concepts.name: Digital Forensics

concepts.definition: Static and dynamic examination of hostile code to learn what it does.
concepts.name: Malware Analysis

concepts.definition: Cloud accounts, roles and policies — identity is the perimeter now.
concepts.name: Identity & Access Management

concepts.definition: Blast-radius control: a breach in one segment does not reach the rest.
concepts.name: Network Segmentation

concepts.definition: No network location is trusted; every request authenticates and authorizes on its own.
concepts.name: Zero Trust

concepts.definition: Keys and tokens out of source control and into something that can rotate them.
concepts.name: Secrets Management

concepts.definition: What is inside the image, where it came from, and what the runtime can reach.
concepts.name: Container Security

concepts.definition: RBAC, network policy and admission control on a cluster that will schedule anything.
concepts.name: Kubernetes Security

concepts.definition: Reviewing infrastructure the way you review code — before any of it exists.
concepts.name: Infrastructure as Code Security

concepts.definition: Everything you did not write but ship anyway: dependencies, images, build systems.
concepts.name: Supply Chain Security

concepts.definition: A bill of materials for software, so “are we affected?” has an answer today.
concepts.name: SBOM

concepts.definition: Ranking what to fix by what it would actually cost you.
concepts.name: Risk Assessment

concepts.definition: The loop from discovery to patch, with owners and dates attached.
concepts.name: Vulnerability Management

concepts.definition: The shared identifier for a known flaw, and the score everyone argues about.
concepts.name: CVE & CVSS

concepts.definition: SOC 2, ISO 27001, PCI DSS — controls somebody else will audit you against.
concepts.name: Compliance Frameworks

concepts.definition: Obligations to collect less, keep it shorter, and guard what is left.
concepts.name: Privacy & Data Protection

concepts.definition: Untrusted text reaching a model that can act: injection, for the LLM era.
concepts.name: Prompt Injection Defense

concepts.definition: Policy checks around a model's inputs and outputs, outside the model itself.
concepts.name: Guardrails

concepts.definition: Inputs perturbed just enough to flip a model's answer while looking unchanged.
concepts.name: Adversarial Examples

concepts.definition: Corrupting training data so the model learns the attacker's rule as if it were yours.
concepts.name: Data Poisoning

concepts.definition: Rebuilding a model you do not own, one query at a time.
concepts.name: Model Extraction

concepts.definition: Weights, datasets and inference stacks you did not build and cannot fully inspect.
concepts.name: AI Supply Chain
